title: Hot-standby KV cache warmup + global circuit-breaker failover postmortem
creator: Aisha Patel
summary: On 2026-03-09 a multi-region failover to the hot-standby (eu-west) region coincided with KV cache warmup and a mis-scoped global circuit breaker, producing a sustained latency SLO miss and aggressive load shedding. This incident review documents timeline, root causes, immediate mitigations, and a prioritized remediation plan to prevent recurrence.
incident_timeline: 2026-03-09T01:12Z - Primary (us-east) experienced gradual CPU pressure following an autoscaling lag after a large customer burst; latency climbed but error rates remained low.
2026-03-09T01:24Z - Smart routing policy triggered automatic regional failover to hot-standby eu-west based on latency SLO threshold configured for the tenant.
2026-03-09T01:25Z - eu-west instances started serving traffic but observed KV cache cold-start behavior: prefix cache hit rate fell from ~92% to ~12%.

2026-03-09T01:27Z - Global circuit breaker detected elevated p95 latency aggregated across regions and tripped to 'global-protect' mode, rerouting many requests to a small set of fallback CPUs in us-central.
2026-03-09T01:28Z - Fallback routing created resource contention and request queuing; autoscaler reacted but with policy cooldowns resulting in underprovisioning for ~18 minutes.
2026-03-09T01:45Z - Load-shedding policy (configured to protect request fairness) began returning 429s aggressively due to queue depth thresholds being hit while KV caching warmed up.
2026-03-09T02:05Z - On-call engineers disabled global circuit breaker to allow region-local routing and manually increased eu-west pool size; p95 latency returned under SLO by 02:18Z.
2026-03-09T02:30Z - Traffic normalized and monitoring showed KV cache hit rate recovering to expected levels after proactive prewarming jobs were added.
impact_metrics: SLO missed: generation.p95 latency exceeded 350ms objective for 51 minutes
Customer-visible 429s: 2.7% of requests returned 429 during peak window
Error rate increase: 5xx rose from baseline 0.03% to 0.6% (peak)
Affected customers: 12 high-traffic tenants experienced degraded tail latency or transient errors
root_cause: Three interacting failures: (1) failover to hot-standby region without prewarming KV/prefix caches, (2) a global circuit-breaker aggregation rule that tripped based on combined cross-region p95 and routed traffic into a constrained fallback, and (3) autoscaler cooldowns + conservative burst capacity settings prevented rapid capacity ramp-up.
contributing_factors: Circuit breaker threshold used global p95 aggregation rather than per-region signals
No automatic KV cache prewarm step was part of the failover playbook for hot-standby instances
Reserved burst capacity for hot-standby was too small to absorb the immediate post-failover load
Load-shedding policy uses static queue thresholds that are sensitive to transient cache warmups
Runbook playbooks did not clearly specify order: increase pool vs disable CB vs prewarm cache
detection: SLO alerts (p95 > 350ms) and synthetic checks flagged the issue. Pager duty alerted on escalation. Circuit-breaker dashboard also showed the global trip before runbook action was taken.
immediate_mitigation: Manually disabled global circuit breaker to restore region-local routing (02:05Z)
Manually scaled up eu-west GPU pool by 2x from reserved capacity (02:06Z)
Launched ad-hoc KV prewarm job to populate prefix/KV cache for the top 500 prefixes (02:08Z)
Temporarily relaxed static load-shedding thresholds to reduce 429s while capacity increased (02:10Z)
permanent_remediation: Change circuit-breaker aggregation to be region-local by default and add a configurable global-mode with stricter guardrails
Add automated KV/prefix cache prewarm step tied to failover events and autoscaler scale-up completion
Increase hot-standby reserved burst capacity and add graduated burst policy for the first 10 minutes after failover
Make load-shedding thresholds adaptive to cache-hit metrics (avoid aggressive 429s during warmups)
Reduce autoscaler cooldown in failover scenarios and add a fast-path scaling policy for emergency widenings
Add a deterministic failover checklist in runbook that orders: (1) prewarm, (2) increase pool, (3) enable region routing, (4) adjust shedding thresholds

monitoring_changes: Add per-region circuit-breaker trip alerts (severity: P1)
Emit prefix cache warmup progress metric with estimated time-to-warm metric
Add synthetic traffic that measures KV-optimal warmup path and expected p95 behavior post-failover

rollout_plan: Remediations will be implemented in stages: stage 1 (2 weeks) - region-local CB and KV prewarm infra; stage 2 (4 weeks) - adaptive load-shedding + burst capacity changes; stage 3 (8 weeks) - autoscaler fast-path and canary failover exercises. Each stage includes a PR review, staging rollout, and production canary for a single tenant before wide rollout.
verification_plan: Run simulated failovers in staging with synthetic traffic and assert p95 remains under SLO within 5 minutes
Post-deploy canary failover for 1 low-traffic tenant and monitor prefix hit rates and error rates for 24 hours
Runbook tabletop and live DR exercise within 6 weeks and capture time-to-recovery metrics
postmortem_notes: Decision: Default circuit-breaker behavior will switch to region-local; global aggregation must be opt-in with stricter cooldowns
Trade-off: Increasing reserved burst capacity has cost implications but reduces customer-visible SLO risk during failover; finance OK'd a temporary increase pending telemetry review
We accepted temporary manual intervention (disabling CB) as necessary but aim to remove manual steps via automation in the remediation roadmap
We will prioritize prewarm infra over complex adaptive shedding in the near term because warmup explains the majority of tail latency
